newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Britain stress convergence on EU reform.
newsitem.headline: France, Britain stress convergence on EU reform.

text.p: France and Britain said on Thursday their views converged on many aspects of European Union reform and they shared a determination to build a more effective common foreign and security policy.

Meeting two days before EU leaders hold a brainstorming summit in Dublin, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said he and British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind were very close on key issues in the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) on reforming EU institutions.
"I would like to lay to rest the cliche that Britain and France are at the antipodes, at opposite ends of the scale from each other expressing two different philosophies," de Charette said.
"Judging by the work we have done today, that idea is simply not right," he said.

He cited similar approaches to making the EU's foreign and defence policy more effective, applying the principle of subsidiarity to stop Brussels handling matters that can be handled at local or national level, giving national parliaments more say in European affairs and reforming the weighted voting system and the European Commission, the EU executive.
Rifkind agreed that their views converged across "a crucial range of issues" in the negotiations, citing the same points.

Both ministers agreed on the importance of sticking to the timetable for concluding a treaty next June to make the EU function more efficiently, so that negotiations to admit central European countries can begin in 1998.
Neither referred to issues on which they disagree, including the planned single European currency and extending the scope of majority voting.
In a conciliatory gesture to Paris, which pressed for Saturday's informal EU summit described by London as unnecessary, Rifkind said:

"I believe the summit in Dublin this Saturday could be a very viable opportunity for the heads of government to speak freely amongst themselves and explore ideas...when it is not necessary to take immediate decisions."

He said that since France and Britain were the two EU powers with global foreign policy interests and military reach, any credible European policy in those areas would have to be built on the closest Franco-British cooperation.
